newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian ANZ job ads fall 0.4 pct in Sept.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian ANZ job ads fall 0.4 pct in Sept.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group (ANZ) said on Monday that its job advertisement series fell by a seasonally adjusted 0.4 percent in September, taking them to their lowest level since January 1994.
Job ads have fallen in six of the first nine months of 1996, and are 14.3 percent lower than the September 1995 level, the ANZ said.
"Demand for labour remains soft, with no signs as yet of a turnaround in hiring intentions following the August budget," ANZ chief economist Saul Eslake said.
In trend terms, job ads fell by 1.1 percent, representing a deterioration in the underlying trend from August, the ANZ said. The trend series has been negative since February 1995.

The decling trend in the series over the past few months suggested employment growth over the next six months was likely to average less than 5,000 jobs per month, compared with growth of 7,500 a month in the six months to August, Eslake said.
"If employment does grow by an average of only 5,000 per month over the next six months, then unemployment may well exceed 9.0 percent of the labour force by early 1997," he said.
He said this would also depend on the number of new entrants to the labour force, which had been particulary volatile in recent months.
Job ads declined in all states except South Australia and Tasmania, where they rose by 20.6 percent and 13.1 percent respectively.
South Australia is the only state where job ads are trending up, and where the number of job ads was higher than in September last year, the ANZ said.

The ANZ also said their previous research which suggested job ads led the official employment data by about six months, with annual growth in the series "explaining" about two-thirds of the annual growth rate in official employment data six months later.

However, research by the Australia Treasury suggested the level of job ads, rather than their rate of change, may be a better leading indicator, and the ANZ said it would detail its findings in a publication next month.
